title: Feature request: multimodal episode ingestion (images, video, audio)
body:
Feature request: multimodal episode ingestion (images, video, audio)

Labels: feature request enhancement

Summary

Graphiti currently only supports text-based episode ingestion. With the release of Google's Gemini Embedding 2 — the first natively multimodal embedding model that maps text, images, video, and audio into a single unified vector space — there is now a strong case for Graphiti to support raw multimodal inputs as first-class episode sources. This would unlock direct visual and audio memory in agentic systems without requiring lossy text translation as an intermediary step.

Background & motivation

I am building a real-time multimodal AI assistant that uses Graphiti as its long-term memory layer. Users can interact via voice, share their screens, upload images, and use live camera input. Currently, my pipeline handles visual inputs by:

  1. Running a vision LLM to generate a text description of the image or frame
  2. Storing the text description as a Graphiti episode
  3. Saving a reference pointer (asset_id) to the raw asset in object storage as episode metadata

This works, but introduces what I'd call a "translation tax" — semantic information present in the raw visual (spatial layout, colour relationships, visual structure) is lost when converting to text before embedding. With Gemini Embedding 2 now available as a Graphiti-supported embedder, that translation step is no longer necessary for the embedding layer — but episode ingestion still only accepts text.

Proposed approach

A two-layer design that preserves full backward compatibility:

Layer 1 — Entity extraction (always text)

When a multimodal episode is ingested, Graphiti passes the raw asset to a vision-capable LLM to generate a structured text description. This text is used for entity and edge extraction — identical to the current behaviour. This layer stays text-based since LLM graph extraction inherently requires language.

Layer 2 — Embedding (multimodal if the configured embedder supports it)

After nodes and edges are extracted, Graphiti calls the configured embedder with the raw asset rather than just the text description — if the embedder supports multimodal input (e.g. GeminiEmbedderConfig). This stores a direct visual or audio vector on the node alongside or instead of the text-derived embedding, enabling native cross-modal similarity retrieval.

Graceful degradation

If the configured embedder is text-only, Graphiti falls back to embedding the generated text description — existing behaviour, no breaking changes.

Desired episode input types

Type | Formats | Use case -- | -- | -- Images | PNG, JPEG | Screenshots, uploads, camera frames Video clips | MP4, MOV | Short screen recordings, keyframe sequences Audio | WAV, MP3 | Native speech embedding without STT as intermediary Documents | PDF | Already partially supported, could extend naturally

Why this matters now

Gemini Embedding 2 (released March 2026) is the first embedding model to natively map text, images, video, and audio into a single unified vector space. This means:

  • A screenshot and a spoken description of it would have comparable vectors without any manual alignment
  • Drift detection and similarity retrieval built on top of Graphiti would work cross-modally out of the box
  • The "translation tax" of vision-LLM-to-text is eliminated at the embedding layer

Since Graphiti already supports GeminiEmbedderConfig, the embedder infrastructure is already in place. The gap is purely at the episode ingestion level.

Questions for the team

  1. Is multimodal episode ingestion on the roadmap at all?
  2. Would a PR scoping only image support (as the simplest starting point) be welcome?
  3. Is there a preferred approach for how the EmbedderClient interface should be extended to signal multimodal capability to the ingestion layer?
  4. Should multimodal embeddings be stored as a separate field alongside name_embedding / fact_embedding, or replace them when a multimodal embedder is configured?

References

  • Gemini Embedding 2 announcement — Google Developers Blog
  • Gemini Embedding 2 API docs
  • Related limitation noted in docs: text-only episode processing
author: Enoch-015

title: [BUG] `edge_similarity_search` crashes on edges with null/invalid `fact_embedding`
body:
# Graphiti Bug Report: `edge_similarity_search` crashes on edges with null/invalid `fact_embedding`

## Bug Description

When a Neo4j graph grows over time, `edge_similarity_search` fails with `Neo.ClientError.Statement.ArgumentError` because some `RELATES_TO` edges have a `null`, empty, or dimension-mismatched `fact_embedding` property. The `vector.similarity.cosine()` function in Neo4j does not accept `null` or invalid vectors, causing the entire search query to fail.

The root cause is in `Neo4jSearchOperations.edge_similarity_search` (`graphiti_core/driver/neo4j/operations/search_ops.py`), which builds a Cypher query that computes cosine similarity on **all** matched edges without first filtering out edges where `fact_embedding` is `null` or invalid:

```cypher
MATCH (n:Entity)-[e:RELATES_TO]->(m:Entity)
WHERE e.group_id IN $group_ids
WITH DISTINCT e, n, m, vector.similarity.cosine(e.fact_embedding, $search_vector) AS score
WHERE score > $min_score
...
```

The same issue likely affects `node_similarity_search` (with `n.name_embedding`) and `community_similarity_search` (with `c.name_embedding`).

## Steps to Reproduce

```python
from graphiti_core import Graphiti

# Initialize Graphiti with Neo4j and a custom embedder
client = Graphiti(
    uri="bolt://localhost:7687",
    user="neo4j",
    password="password",
    llm_client=my_llm_adapter,
    embedder=my_embedder_adapter,  # e.g., 1024-dim embeddings
)
await client.build_indices_and_constraints()

# Add multiple episodes over time — some embedding calls may silently fail
# or edges may be created with null/mismatched fact_embedding
for episode in episodes:
    await client.add_episode(
        name=episode.name,
        episode_body=episode.body,
        source_description=episode.description,
        reference_time=episode.timestamp,
        group_id="user_123",
    )

# Eventually, search fails when it encounters an edge with invalid embedding
results = await client.search(
    query="list today's emails",
    group_ids=["user_123"],
    limit=50,
)
# ^ Raises Neo.ClientError.Statement.ArgumentError
```

## Expected Behavior

The search query should gracefully skip edges (and nodes) where the embedding property is `null` or invalid, and return results only from edges with valid embeddings. A `WHERE e.fact_embedding IS NOT NULL` clause (or equivalent) should be added before the `vector.similarity.cosine()` call.

## Actual Behavior

The entire search query fails with:

```
neo4j.exceptions.ClientError: {neo4j_code: Neo.ClientError.Statement.ArgumentError}
{message: Invalid input for 'vector.similarity.cosine()': Argument a is not a valid vector for this similarity function.}
```

This causes complete search failure — no results are returned, even though most edges have valid embeddings.

## Environment

- **Graphiti Version**: 0.28.0 (also verified code is unchanged in 0.28.2)
- **Python Version**: 3.12
- **Operating System**: Linux (Docker container)
- **Database Backend**: Neo4j 5.x (via `neo4j==6.1.0` Python driver)
- **LLM Provider & Model**: Custom LLM adapter (T-Systems OTC / `text-embedding-bge-m3`, 1024 dimensions)

## Installation Method

- [x] pip install

## Error Messages/Traceback

```
ERROR: Error executing Neo4j query: {neo4j_code: Neo.ClientError.Statement.ArgumentError} {message: Invalid input for 'vector.similarity.cosine()': Argument a is not a valid vector for this similarity function.} {gql_status: 22N38} {gql_status_description: error: data exception - invalid function argument. Invalid argument to the function vector.similarity.cosine.}
        MATCH (n:Entity)-[e:RELATES_TO]->(m:Entity)
     WHERE e.group_id IN $group_ids
            WITH DISTINCT e, n, m, vector.similarity.cosine(e.fact_embedding, $search_vector) AS score
            WHERE score > $min_score
            RETURN
            e.uuid AS uuid,
            n.uuid AS source_node_uuid,
            m.uuid AS target_node_uuid,
            ...
            ORDER BY score DESC
            LIMIT $limit

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../graphiti_core/search/search_utils.py", line 431, in edge_similarity_search
    records, _, _ = await driver.execute_query(
  ...
  File ".../neo4j/_async/io/_common.py", line 263, in on_failure
    raise self._hydrate_error(metadata)
neo4j.exceptions.ClientError: {neo4j_code: Neo.ClientError.Statement.ArgumentError}
{message: Invalid input for 'vector.similarity.cosine()': Argument a is not a valid vector for this similarity function.}
```

## Configuration

```python
# Custom embedder producing 1024-dim vectors (bge-m3)
# Graphiti initialized with:
client = Graphiti(
    uri="bolt://neo4j:7687",
    user="neo4j",
    password="***",
    llm_client=amas_llm_adapter,
    embedder=amas_embedder_adapter,  # 1024-dim
)
```

## Additional Context

- **Consistency**: Happens consistently once the graph has enough edges — as the graph grows, the probability of encountering an edge with a null/invalid `fact_embedding` increases. Small graphs may work fine.
- **Component**: Core library (`graphiti-core`)
- **Root cause**: Edges can end up with `null` or invalid `fact_embedding` when:
  1. The embedding API call fails/times out during `add_episode()` but the edge itself is still created in Neo4j
  2. A different embedding model with different dimensions was used at some point (dimension mismatch)
  3. The embedding returns NaN values (related: [#945](https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/issues/945))
- **Related issues**: [#945 - Custom OPENAI_BASE_URL causes NaN embeddings](https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/issues/945), [neo4j/graph-data-science#26 - Cosine similarity with null value](https://github.com/neo4j/graph-data-science/issues/26)
- **Scope**: Affects `edge_similarity_search`, and potentially `node_similarity_search` and `community_similarity_search` in the same file

## Possible Solution

Add a `WHERE` clause to filter out edges/nodes with null embeddings **before** computing cosine similarity. For `edge_similarity_search` in `neo4j/operations/search_ops.py`:

```cypher
MATCH (n:Entity)-[e:RELATES_TO]->(m:Entity)
WHERE e.group_id IN $group_ids
  AND e.fact_embedding IS NOT NULL
  AND size(e.fact_embedding) = size($search_vector)
WITH DISTINCT e, n, m, vector.similarity.cosine(e.fact_embedding, $search_vector) AS score
WHERE score > $min_score
...
```

The fix should be applied to all three similarity search methods:
1. `edge_similarity_search` → guard `e.fact_embedding`
2. `node_similarity_search` → guard `n.name_embedding`
3. `community_similarity_search` → guard `c.name_embedding`

Additionally, consider adding a data validation/cleanup utility to detect and optionally re-embed or remove edges/nodes with invalid embeddings.

title: [BUG] FalkorDB: add_episode() mutates shared self.driver causing cross-group data contamination
body:
## Bug Description

When multiple `group_id` episodes are processed concurrently (e.g., via the MCP server's per-group queue workers), `add_episode()` mutates `self.driver` on the shared `Graphiti` instance, causing data to be written to the wrong FalkorDB graph.

## Root Cause

In `graphiti.py`, lines 887-889 of `add_episode()`:

```python
if group_id != self.driver._database:
    self.driver = self.driver.clone(database=group_id)
    self.clients.driver = self.driver
```

This mutates the shared instance's `self.driver`. When two async tasks call `add_episode()` concurrently with different group_ids (e.g., `patroni` and `cicd`), they race to reassign `self.driver`. Whichever runs last wins, and the other task's writes go to the wrong FalkorDB graph.

## Reproduction

```python
import asyncio
from graphiti_core import Graphiti

graphiti = Graphiti(...)  # FalkorDB backend

# Concurrent add_episode calls with different group_ids
await asyncio.gather(
    graphiti.add_episode(name="ep1", episode_body="data for group A", group_id="group_a", ...),
    graphiti.add_episode(name="ep2", episode_body="data for group B", group_id="group_b", ...),
)

# Result: ep1's nodes may end up in the "group_b" FalkorDB graph (or vice versa)
```

Verified via direct FalkorDB query:
```bash
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY group_a "MATCH (n) RETURN n.name, n.group_id LIMIT 10"
# Shows nodes with group_id="group_b" — cross-contaminated
```

## Impact

- Data silently written to wrong FalkorDB graph
- Search returns incomplete results (data is in a different graph than expected)
- `clear_graph` fails to clean up (nodes have mismatched group_id vs actual graph location)
- Affects the MCP server which uses per-group async queue workers sharing one Graphiti instance

## Proposed Fix

`add_episode()` should use a local driver clone instead of mutating `self.driver`:

```python
if group_id != self.driver._database:
    driver = self.driver.clone(database=group_id)
else:
    driver = self.driver
# Use `driver` for all operations in this call, don't assign to self
```

## Workaround

Serialize all `add_episode()` calls through a single global queue (no concurrent processing across groups).

## Related

- #1161 — FalkorDB search fails with single group_id
- #1325 / #1326 — handle_multiple_group_ids skips graph routing for single group_id

Both issues share the same root architectural problem: FalkorDB uses separate graph databases per group_id, but the driver selection is done via shared mutable state.

title: Bug: --host and --port CLI flags ignored by apply_cli_overrides
body:
## Description

The `--host` and `--port` CLI flags for `graphiti-mcp-server` are parsed by argparse but never applied to the config. The server always binds to `0.0.0.0:8000` regardless of what's passed.

## Root Cause

In `mcp_server/src/config/schema.py`, `apply_cli_overrides()` handles transport, LLM, embedder, database, and graphiti overrides but skips `host` and `port`:

https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/blob/main/mcp_server/src/config/schema.py

The CLI flags are defined in `graphiti_mcp_server.py`:
```python
parser.add_argument('--host', help='Host to bind the MCP server to')
parser.add_argument('--port', type=int, help='Port to bind the MCP server to')
```

But `apply_cli_overrides` never applies them:
```python
def apply_cli_overrides(self, args) -> None:
    # Override server settings
    if hasattr(args, 'transport') and args.transport:
        self.server.transport = args.transport
    # ... llm, embedder, database, graphiti overrides
    # host and port are missing
```

So `ServerConfig` defaults always win:
```python
class ServerConfig(BaseModel):
    host: str = Field(default='0.0.0.0', description='Server host')
    port: int = Field(default=8000, description='Server port')
```

## Steps to Reproduce

```bash
graphiti-mcp-server --transport sse --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9999
# Logs show: Running MCP server with SSE transport on 0.0.0.0:8000
```

## Expected Behavior

Server should bind to `127.0.0.1:9999`.

## Suggested Fix

Add the missing overrides in `apply_cli_overrides`:

```python
# Override server settings
if hasattr(args, 'transport') and args.transport:
    self.server.transport = args.transport
if hasattr(args, 'host') and args.host:
    self.server.host = args.host
if hasattr(args, 'port') and args.port:
    self.server.port = args.port
```

## Workaround

Use `SERVER__HOST` and `SERVER__PORT` env vars, which pydantic-settings picks up via `env_nested_delimiter='__'`.

title: FalkorDB: empty fulltext query crashes with RediSearch syntax error when all query words are stopwords
body:
## Problem

When `build_fulltext_query` in `falkordb_driver.py` receives a query where all words are filtered out as stopwords, `sanitized_query` becomes an empty string. The method still constructs the full query string, producing:

\`\`\`
(@group_id:"standups") ()
\`\`\`

The trailing \`()\` is invalid RediSearch syntax and causes FalkorDB to throw:

\`\`\`
RediSearch: Syntax error at offset 24 near standups
\`\`\`

This error surfaces during \`graphiti.add_episode()\` when graphiti internally searches for existing nodes to merge with, and the extracted entity name consists entirely of stopwords.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use a FalkorDB-backed Graphiti instance with a \`group_id\` set (e.g. \`"standups"\`)
2. Ingest an episode where the LLM extracts an entity whose name is composed entirely of RediSearch stopwords (e.g. \`"is"\`, \`"the"\`, \`"a"\`, etc.)
3. Graphiti calls \`build_fulltext_query\` with that entity name — all words are stripped, \`sanitized_query = ""\`
4. The method constructs \`"(@group_id:\\"standups\\") ()"\` and passes it to FalkorDB
5. FalkorDB raises a syntax error

## Fix

Add a guard for the empty-query case before constructing \`full_query\`:

\`\`\`python
# If the query is empty (all words were stopwords) or too long, return no query
if not sanitized_query:
    return ''
\`\`\`

This should be inserted before the existing \`max_query_length\` check in \`build_fulltext_query\` (~line 419 in \`falkordb_driver.py\`).

## Version

- \`graphiti-core\`: 0.28.2
- FalkorDB driver

title: [BUG]  `episode_mentions_reranker` sorts nodes ascending (fewest mentions first)
body:
## Bug Description
`episode_mentions_reranker` in `graphiti_core/search/search_utils.py` sorts nodes in ascending order of mention count, so nodes mentioned in the fewest episodes rank highest. This is the opposite of what the reranker name implies and what the equivalent edge reranker does.

## Steps to Reproduce
Provide a minimal code example that reproduces the issue:

```python
from collections import defaultdict                                                        

def rrf(results, rank_const=1, min_score=0):
    scores = defaultdict(float)
    for result in results:
        for i, uuid in enumerate(result):
            scores[uuid] += 1 / (i + rank_const)                                                        
    sorted_uuids = sorted(scores.keys(), key=lambda u: scores[u], reverse=True)
    return (                                                                                            
        [u for u in sorted_uuids if scores[u] >= min_score],                                          
        [scores[u] for u in sorted_uuids if scores[u] >= min_score],                                    
    )                                                                                                 

# Simulate episode_mentions_reranker with mocked DB counts                                              
def simulate_reranker(node_uuid_lists, db_mention_counts):
    sorted_uuids, _ = rrf(node_uuid_lists)                                                              
    scores = {}                                                                                         
    for uuid in sorted_uuids:                                                                           
        if uuid in db_mention_counts:                                                                   
            scores[uuid] = db_mention_counts[uuid]                                                    
    for uuid in sorted_uuids:                                                                           
        if uuid not in scores:                                                                          
            scores[uuid] = float('inf')                                                                 
    sorted_uuids.sort(key=lambda u: scores[u])  # line 1894 — ascending                                 
    return [(u, scores[u]) for u in sorted_uuids]                                                       
                                                                                                          
result = simulate_reranker(                                                                             
    [["node-A", "node-B", "node-C"]],                                                                   
    {"node-A": 20, "node-B": 5, "node-C": 1},                                                           
)                                                                                                       
for rank, (uuid, score) in enumerate(result, 1):                                                        
    print(f"rank {rank}: {uuid}  mentions={score}")
```

## Expected Behavior
```
rank 1: node-A  mentions=20                                                                           
rank 2: node-B  mentions=5                                                                              
rank 3: node-C  mentions=1
```

## Actual Behavior
```
rank 1: node-C  mentions=1                                                                           
rank 2: node-B  mentions=5                                                                           
rank 3: node-A  mentions=20
```

## Environment
- **Graphiti Version**: current `main`
- **Python Version**: any
- **Operating System**: any
- **Database Backend**: any
- **LLM Provider & Model**: any

## Installation Method
- [x] Development installation (git clone)

## Error Messages/Traceback
No exception is raised. The output is silently wrong.

## Additional Context
This is a copy-paste bug from node_distance_reranker. A stray comment on line 1875 is the tell:         

`async def episode_mentions_reranker(...)`:
```python                                                                         
# Find the shortest path to center node   <- copy-pasted from node_distance_reranker                 
sorted_uuids.sort(key=lambda cur_uuid: scores[cur_uuid])   
```                                         
                               
Ascending sort is correct in node_distance_reranker because the score is a graph distance (smaller =    
closer = better, then inverted before returning). It is wrong here because the score is a raw mention   
count (larger = more prominent = better).                                                               
                                                                                                      
The edge `episode_mentions` path in `search.py` shows the correct intent - it explicitly adds reverse=True  
after sorting:

```python                                                                
# search.py:304-305                                                                                   
if config.reranker == EdgeReranker.episode_mentions:                                                    
    reranked_edges.sort(reverse=True, key=lambda edge: len(edge.episodes))
```

The node path has no equivalent correction at the call site in `node_search`:

```python
# search.py:401-417
elif config.reranker == NodeReranker.episode_mentions:
    reranked_uuids, node_scores = await episode_mentions_reranker(
        driver, search_result_uuids, min_score=reranker_min_score
    )
elif config.reranker == NodeReranker.node_distance:
    if center_node_uuid is None:
        raise SearchRerankerError('No center node provided for Node Distance reranker')
    reranked_uuids, node_scores = await node_distance_reranker(
        driver,
        rrf(search_result_uuids, min_score=reranker_min_score)[0],
        center_node_uuid,
        min_score=reranker_min_score,
    )

reranked_nodes = [node_uuid_map[uuid] for uuid in reranked_uuids]

return reranked_nodes[:limit], node_scores[:limit]
```
                                                                                                        
The existing test does not catch this (`tests/utils/search/search_utils_test.py::test_episode_mentions_reranker`) because it only compares a node with 1 mention against a node with 0 mentions. The zero-mention node is absent from the DB result and receives the sentinel `float('inf')`. Under ascending sort 1 < inf, so the mentioned node ranks first by accident. The bug only manifests when two nodes both have positive mention counts.

The `float('inf')` sentinel interacts with the fix. A pure `reverse=True` patch moves zero-mention nodes    
(`inf`) to rank first. The correct fix changes both the sentinel and the sort direction.
                                                                
- Affects: core library, NodeReranker.episode_mentions search config                                    
- Occurs consistently on any graph where multiple nodes each appear in at least one episode

## Possible Solution
```py
# search_utils.py:1889-1898
for uuid in sorted_uuids:                                                                             
    if uuid not in scores:
        scores[uuid] = 0  # was float('inf') - keeps zero-mention nodes at the bottom after fix
                                                                                                        
sorted_uuids.sort(key=lambda cur_uuid: scores[cur_uuid], reverse=True)  # was ascending                 
                                                                                                        
return [uuid for uuid in sorted_uuids if scores[uuid] >= min_score], [                                  
    scores[uuid] for uuid in sorted_uuids if scores[uuid] >= min_score                                
]
```                                                                                                       

The test should also be extended with a second episodic node and edge so that both entity nodes have a  
positive mention count, then assert the more-mentioned node ranks first.

title: Agent identity for knowledge graph attribution
body:
## Summary

Knowledge graph nodes contributed by agents need identity — without it you can't track provenance or control which agents can modify the graph.

AgentID provides cryptographic identity for AI agents — ECDSA P-256 certificates, Ed25519 key binding, verification API, trust scoring.

**Proven:**
- 3 ratified specs in the Agent Identity Working Group (QSP-1, DID Resolution, Entity Verification) — all unanimous
- Code merged into corpollc/qntm (encrypted relay protocol)
- Integrations: CrewAI, LangChain, MCP, OpenAI Agents SDK
- Registered issuer in the Open Agent Trust Registry

Source: [github.com/haroldmalikfrimpong-ops/getagentid](https://github.com/haroldmalikfrimpong-ops/getagentid)

Happy to contribute an integration.

title: bug(mcp): read tools reject scalar group_ids even in single-workspace use cases
body:
Passing a single workspace id to the MCP read tools currently fails validation even though the intent is clear.

For example, calls like `search_memory_facts(query="...", group_ids="ideadb")` or `get_episodes(group_ids="ideadb")` error out because the server only accepts `group_ids` as a list. That works, but it’s awkward for the common single-workspace case and it breaks clients that surface scalar inputs for simple tool calls.

I think the server should accept either form:
- `group_ids=["ideadb"]`
- `group_ids="ideadb"`

and normalize the string form internally.

I’ve opened a PR with a small patch that does exactly that for `search_nodes`, `search_memory_facts`, `get_episodes`, and `clear_graph`, along with focused tests.

title: [BUG] label_propagation infinite loop when entity pairs have edge_count >= 2
body:
## Bug Description

`build_communities()` hangs indefinitely (100% CPU, never returns) when the graph contains entity pairs connected by 2 or more `RELATES_TO` edges. This is a common condition in real workloads — multiple episodes referencing the same two entities naturally produce `edge_count >= 2`.

The root cause is an infinite loop in `label_propagation()` inside `graphiti_core/utils/maintenance/community_operations.py`. The original `while True` loop has two conflicting update branches that oscillate forever without converging when `edge_count >= 2`.

## Steps to Reproduce

```python
import asyncio
from graphiti_core import Graphiti
from graphiti_core.nodes import EpisodeType
from datetime import datetime, timezone

# After initializing client...

# Add episodes that cause multiple RELATES_TO edges between the same entity pairs
episodes = [
    "Zhang San joined Company A in January 2024 as a software engineer.",
    "Li Si has been working at Company A since 2023. Li Si and Zhang San are teammates.",
    "Company A is a Beijing-based technology company with about 50 engineers.",
]
for i, text in enumerate(episodes):
    await client.add_episode(
        name=f"ep{i}",
        episode_body=text,
        source=EpisodeType.text,
        source_description="test",
        reference_time=datetime(2024, 1, 15, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
        group_id="test_group",
    )

# This hangs forever — 100% CPU, no output, no error
await client.build_communities(group_ids=["test_group"])
```

The bug can also be reproduced in pure Python without any database:

```python
from collections import defaultdict
from graphiti_core.utils.maintenance.community_operations import Neighbor, label_propagation

# Two nodes with edge_count=2 — the minimal trigger
projection = {
    "A": [Neighbor(node_uuid="B", edge_count=2)],
    "B": [Neighbor(node_uuid="A", edge_count=2)],
}

# This never returns
label_propagation(projection)
```

## Expected Behavior

`build_communities()` should complete and return community nodes. `label_propagation()` should always terminate regardless of `edge_count` values.

## Actual Behavior

`build_communities()` hangs indefinitely with the Python process pinned at 100% CPU. There is no error, no traceback, and no output. The process must be killed manually.

The pure-Python reproduction shows the oscillation clearly (capped at 8 rounds to prevent actual hanging):

```
round 1: {'A': 1, 'B': 0}
round 2: {'A': 0, 'B': 1}  <- back to initial state!
round 3: {'A': 1, 'B': 0}
round 4: {'A': 0, 'B': 1}
...
❌ INFINITE LOOP: still oscillating after 8 rounds
```

After adding the episodes above, Neo4j shows:
```
Entity pairs with edge_count >= 2 (trigger condition):
  Li Si      -- Zhang San   edge_count=2
  Zhang San  -- Li Si       edge_count=2
```

Calling `build_communities()` with a 10s timeout:
```
[process hung here — killed after 10s with no output or error]
```

## Root Cause

In `label_propagation()`, the `while True` loop has two conflicting branches:

```python
while True:
    ...
    for uuid, neighbors in projection.items():
        ...
        if community_candidate != -1 and candidate_rank > 1:
            new_community = community_candidate      # branch A: ID can DECREASE
        else:
            new_community = max(community_candidate, curr_community)  # branch B: ID can only INCREASE
    ...
    if no_change:
        break
    community_map = new_community_map
```

When `edge_count >= 2`, `candidate_rank > 1` is true so **branch A** is taken. Branch A can assign a lower community ID. In the next iteration, **branch B** (`max()`) pulls the ID back up. These two opposing forces cause the map to oscillate and `no_change` is never `True`.

## Environment

- **Graphiti Version**: 0.28.2
- **Python Version**: 3.13
- **Operating System**: macOS
- **Database Backend**: Neo4j 5.x
- **LLM Provider & Model**: DeepSeek deepseek-chat (via OpenAI-compatible API)

## Installation Method

- [x] pip install

## Error Messages/Traceback

```
No error or traceback — the process hangs silently at 100% CPU.
```

## Configuration

```python
client = Graphiti(
    uri=NEO4J_URI,
    user=NEO4J_USER,
    password=NEO4J_PASSWORD,
    llm_client=llm_client,
    embedder=embedder,
)

# Hangs here:
await client.build_communities(group_ids=["test_group"])
```

## Additional Context

- Happens **consistently** whenever `edge_count >= 2` exists between any entity pair in the group.
- Affects the **core library** (`build_communities()` → `get_community_clusters()` → `label_propagation()`).
- Any real-world incremental usage will eventually produce `edge_count >= 2` — multiple episodes mentioning the same two entities is normal.
- Component: core library.

## Possible Solution

Replace `while True` with a bounded `for` loop. The algorithm logic is completely unchanged — only the termination guarantee is added. The loop still breaks early on convergence exactly as before.

```python
# FIX START: replace `while True` with a bounded loop to prevent infinite
# oscillation when candidate_rank > 1 causes IDs to decrease while the
# max() fallback in the else-branch causes them to increase, creating a
# cycle that never satisfies no_change == True.
max_iterations = len(projection) * 10 + 10
for _ in range(max_iterations):
# FIX END
    no_change = True
    new_community_map: dict[str, int] = {}

    for uuid, neighbors in projection.items():
        ...

    # FIX START: update community_map before the break check so the last
    # iteration's result is preserved when the loop exits at max_iterations.
    community_map = new_community_map

    if no_change:
        break
    # FIX END
```

With this fix, the pure-Python reproduction converges immediately, and `build_communities()` completes successfully and creates community nodes correctly.

I have a fix ready in a PR.

title: KuzuDriver missing _database attribute causes AttributeError in add_episode
body:
## Description

`Graphiti.add_episode()` references `self.driver._database` at [graphiti.py line 887](https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/blob/main/graphiti_core/graphiti.py#L887), but `KuzuDriver` does not set this attribute. This causes an `AttributeError` when calling `add_episode` with a `group_id` parameter.

## Steps to Reproduce

```python
from graphiti_core import Graphiti
from graphiti_core.graphiti import EpisodeType
from graphiti_core.driver.kuzu_driver import KuzuDriver
from datetime import datetime, timezone

driver = KuzuDriver(db="/tmp/test_kuzu")
graphiti = Graphiti(graph_driver=driver)
await graphiti.build_indices_and_constraints()

await graphiti.add_episode(
    name="test",
    episode_body="Ray Dalio founded Bridgewater Associates in 1975.",
    source_description="test",
    reference_time=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
    source=EpisodeType.text,
    group_id="test",
)
```

## Error

```
File "graphiti_core/graphiti.py", line 887, in add_episode
    if group_id != self.driver._database:
AttributeError: 'KuzuDriver' object has no attribute '_database'. Did you mean: 'with_database'?
```

## Analysis

The `_database` attribute is set by Neo4j/FalkorDB/Neptune drivers but not by `KuzuDriver`. The check at line 887 compares `group_id` against `self.driver._database` to decide whether to clone the driver for a different database.

`KuzuDriver.__init__` sets `self.db` (the Kuzu `Database` object) but never sets `self._database` (the string database name).

## Workaround

```python
if not hasattr(driver, "_database"):
    driver._database = driver.default_group_id or "default"
```

## Environment

- graphiti-core: 0.28.2
- kuzu: 0.11.3
- Python: 3.12.4
- macOS arm64

title: KuzuDriver setup_schema does not create FTS indices required by search operations
body:
## Description

`KuzuDriver.setup_schema()` creates the node/edge table schema but does not create the FTS (full-text search) indices that `KuzuSearchOperations` requires. All search methods fail with `Binder exception: Table X doesn't have an index with name Y`.

## Steps to Reproduce

```python
from graphiti_core import Graphiti
from graphiti_core.graphiti import EpisodeType
from graphiti_core.driver.kuzu_driver import KuzuDriver
from datetime import datetime, timezone

driver = KuzuDriver(db="/tmp/test_kuzu")
graphiti = Graphiti(graph_driver=driver)
await graphiti.build_indices_and_constraints()

# Ingest an episode (succeeds after _database workaround from separate issue)
await graphiti.add_episode(
    name="test",
    episode_body="Ray Dalio founded Bridgewater Associates in 1975.",
    source_description="test",
    reference_time=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
    source=EpisodeType.text,
    group_id="test",
)

# Search fails
await graphiti.search(query="Bridgewater", group_ids=["test"], num_results=5)
```

## Error

```
RuntimeError: Binder exception: Table RelatesToNode_ doesn't have an index with name edge_name_and_fact.
CALL QUERY_FTS_INDEX('RelatesToNode_', 'edge_name_and_fact', ...)
```

## Analysis

The search operations reference 4 FTS indices (from `INDEX_TO_LABEL_KUZU_MAPPING` in `graph_queries.py`):

| Table | Index Name | Columns |
|-------|-----------|---------|
| Entity | node_name_and_summary | name, summary |
| Community | community_name | name |
| Episodic | episode_content | content |
| RelatesToNode_ | edge_name_and_fact | name, fact |

These indices are never created. `KuzuDriver.setup_schema()` runs `SCHEMA_QUERIES` which only contains `CREATE NODE TABLE` / `CREATE REL TABLE` statements. `KuzuDriver.build_indices_and_constraints()` is a no-op (`pass`).

The indices need to be created via Kuzu's `CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX()` syntax.

## Workaround

```python
import kuzu

conn = kuzu.Connection(driver.db)
fts_indices = [
    ("Entity", "node_name_and_summary", ["name", "summary"]),
    ("Community", "community_name", ["name"]),
    ("Episodic", "episode_content", ["content"]),
    ("RelatesToNode_", "edge_name_and_fact", ["name", "fact"]),
]
for table, index_name, columns in fts_indices:
    cols = ", ".join(f"'{c}'" for c in columns)
    conn.execute(f"CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('{table}', '{index_name}', [{cols}])")
conn.close()
```

## Suggested Fix

Add FTS index creation to either `setup_schema()` or `build_indices_and_constraints()`:

```python
async def build_indices_and_constraints(self, delete_existing: bool = False):
    conn = kuzu.Connection(self.db)
    for table, index_name, columns in FTS_INDEX_DEFINITIONS:
        cols = ", ".join(f"'{c}'" for c in columns)
        try:
            conn.execute(f"CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('{table}', '{index_name}', [{cols}])")
        except Exception:
            pass  # Index may already exist
    conn.close()
```

## Environment

- graphiti-core: 0.28.2
- kuzu: 0.11.3
- Python: 3.12.4
- macOS arm64

title: [Feature] Optional Bearer token authentication for MCP server
body:
# [Feature] Optional Bearer token authentication for MCP server

## Summary

The Graphiti MCP server currently exposes its HTTP endpoint without any authentication mechanism. When deployed on a network-accessible host, anyone who can reach the port can read, write, and delete knowledge graph data. For example, if the user is running Graphiti as a memory store for personal AI assistants on a laptop, then go to a public wifi network, their data is at risk.

This proposal adds **optional Bearer token authentication** as a simple, opt-in security layer for the MCP HTTP endpoint.

## Motivation

- **Self-hosted deployments are exposed by default.** The MCP server binds to `0.0.0.0:8000` and accepts all requests. In a home-server or cloud deployment, this means any device on the network (or the Internet, if port-forwarded) can access the full API.
- **No existing auth mechanism.** The MCP server has no built-in way to restrict access. Users must rely on network-level controls (firewalls, reverse proxies) which many self-hosters don't configure.
- **MCP clients already support Bearer auth.** Claude Code and other MCP clients support passing an `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header when connecting to HTTP MCP servers, making this a natural fit.

## Proposed Implementation

1. **Opt-in via environment variable:** When `MCP_API_KEY` is set, all HTTP requests must include `Authorization: Bearer <MCP_API_KEY>`. When unset, the server behaves exactly as it does today (no auth).
2. **ASGI middleware approach:** A lightweight `BearerTokenMiddleware` wraps the FastMCP ASGI app (Starlette), checking the `Authorization` header before any request reaches MCP handlers.
3. **Clear error responses:** Returns `401 Unauthorized` with a descriptive message when the token is missing or invalid.
4. **Health endpoint exemption (optional):** The `/health` endpoint could remain unauthenticated to support container orchestration health checks.

## Example implementation

```python
class BearerTokenMiddleware:
    """ASGI middleware that validates Bearer token against MCP_API_KEY env var."""

    def __init__(self, app, api_key: str):
        self.app = app
        self.api_key = api_key

    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
        if scope['type'] == 'http':
            headers = dict(scope.get('headers', []))
            auth = headers.get(b'authorization', b'').decode()
            if not auth.startswith('Bearer ') or auth[7:] != self.api_key:
                response = Response('Unauthorized', status_code=401)
                await response(scope, receive, send)
                return
        await self.app(scope, receive, send)
```

Applied in the FastMCP app factory:

```python
mcp_api_key = os.environ.get('MCP_API_KEY')
if mcp_api_key:
    app = BearerTokenMiddleware(app, mcp_api_key)
```

## Client configuration

With auth enabled, clients connect like:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  graphiti http://host:8000/mcp
```

## Why not use FastMCP's built-in TokenVerifier?

FastMCP already has a `TokenVerifier` protocol and `AuthSettings` for OAuth-based auth. However, this system is designed around full OAuth 2.0 flows:

- `AuthSettings` requires `issuer_url` (an OAuth authorization server URL) and `resource_server_url` — neither of which exist for a simple static token.
- `TokenVerifier.verify_token()` must return an `AccessToken` object with `client_id` and `scopes`, which are meaningless for a static Bearer token.
- The auth system also supports client registration, token exchange, refresh tokens, and revocation — none of which apply here.

Using `TokenVerifier` for a static token would mean fabricating dummy OAuth metadata. A simple ASGI middleware that checks a single env var is more honest, easier to understand, and easier to maintain.

If Graphiti later needs full OAuth support, `TokenVerifier` is the right path. This proposal is specifically for the simpler "shared secret" use case common in self-hosted deployments.


## What this does NOT cover

- OAuth2, API key rotation, or multi-key support — those are more complex and can be added later
- Per-`group_id` authorization — this is a server-level gate, not fine-grained access control
- HTTPS/TLS — that's the responsibility of the deployment environment (reverse proxy, etc.)

## Environment

- Graphiti MCP server (`mcp_server/`)
- Tested with Claude Code MCP client over HTTP transport
- Deployed with Docker, ARM64 + AMD64

title: Expose custom_extraction_instructions in add_memory MCP tool
body:
## Problem

`Graphiti.add_episode()` accepts a `custom_extraction_instructions: str | None` parameter that allows callers to customize entity extraction behavior (e.g., specifying output language, domain-specific entity types, extraction focus).

However, the MCP server's `add_memory` tool does not expose this parameter. It only passes `name`, `episode_body`, `group_id`, `source`, `source_description`, and `uuid` to `queue_service.add_episode()`.

This means MCP clients cannot pass custom extraction instructions to the underlying Graphiti engine.

## Use Case

When ingesting non-English content, entity extraction prompts (which are English-only) cause the LLM to generate summaries and relation names in English, even though the input is in another language. With `custom_extraction_instructions`, callers could instruct the LLM to preserve the input language for summaries and entity names.

Other use cases:
- Domain-specific extraction rules ("focus on financial entities", "ignore personal names")
- Output formatting instructions
- Entity naming conventions

## Current Workaround

Prepending instructions to `source_description`:

```python
source_description = "IMPORTANT: Write summaries in same language as input. " + original
```

This works because `source_description` is included in the extraction prompt context, but it is fragile and mixes metadata with instructions.

## Proposed Change

Add `custom_extraction_instructions` as an optional parameter to the `add_memory` MCP tool and pass it through to `queue_service.add_episode()`:

```python
async def add_memory(
    name: str,
    episode_body: str,
    group_id: str | None = None,
    source: str = 'text',
    source_description: str = '',
    uuid: str | None = None,
    custom_extraction_instructions: str | None = None,  # NEW
) -> SuccessResponse | ErrorResponse:
```

And in the handler:

```python
await queue_service.add_episode(
    ...
    custom_extraction_instructions=custom_extraction_instructions,
)
```

This is a non-breaking, backward-compatible change - existing callers that do not pass the parameter continue to work as before.

title: Audit trail validation for knowledge graph operations
body:
Knowledge graphs that feed agent decisions need strong governance - audit trails for graph mutations, access controls on queries, and error handling around graph operations. Especially when the graph drives real-time agent behavior.

There's no CI-level check to verify these patterns exist in code that integrates graphiti. A scanner that runs on every PR and flags missing logging, error handling, or oversight mechanisms around graph operations would help teams stay compliant.

I built a GitHub Action for agent governance scanning ([asqav-compliance](https://github.com/jagmarques/asqav-compliance)). Would there be interest in governance validation tooling for graphiti, either native or as a recommended CI integration?

title: [BUG] MCP Server: cross_encoder/reranker not configurable, hardcoded to OpenAI — requires OPENAI_API_KEY even with non-OpenAI providers
body:
## Bug Description

The MCP server does not pass a `cross_encoder` argument when constructing the `Graphiti` client. This causes `Graphiti.__init__` to always fall back to `OpenAIRerankerClient()`, which requires `OPENAI_API_KEY`. This makes it impossible to run the MCP server without an OpenAI API key, even when using Anthropic/Gemini/Groq for both LLM and embeddings.

## Steps to Reproduce

Configure the MCP server to use non-OpenAI providers for both LLM and embeddings:

```yaml
# config.yaml
llm:
  provider: "anthropic"
  model: "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001"
  temperature: 0.0
  providers:
    anthropic:
      api_key: "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}"

embedder:
  provider: "gemini"
  model: "gemini-embedding-001"
  providers:
    gemini:
      api_key: "${GOOGLE_API_KEY}"

database:
  provider: "falkordb"
```

Start the MCP server. Both LLM and embedder clients are created successfully, but initialization crashes when `Graphiti.__init__` tries to create the default `OpenAIRerankerClient`.

## Expected Behavior

The MCP server should allow configuring the cross-encoder/reranker provider, or at minimum select a matching reranker based on the configured LLM provider.

## Actual Behavior

The server crashes with:

```
openai.OpenAIError: The api_key client option must be set either by passing api_key to the client or by setting the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable
```

Traceback:

```
File "/app/mcp/src/graphiti_mcp_server.py", line 225, in initialize
    self.client = Graphiti(
File "/app/mcp/.venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/graphiti_core/graphiti.py", line 224, in __init__
    self.cross_encoder = OpenAIRerankerClient()
File "/app/mcp/.venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/graphiti_core/cross_encoder/openai_reranker_client.py", line 55, in __init__
    self.client = AsyncOpenAI(api_key=config.api_key, base_url=config.base_url)
openai.OpenAIError: The api_key client option must be set either by passing api_key to the client or by setting the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable
```

## Environment
- **Graphiti Version**: graphiti-core 0.28.2, MCP server 1.0.2 (Docker image `zepai/knowledge-graph-mcp:1.0.2-graphiti-0.28.2`)
- **Python Version**: 3.11
- **Operating System**: Docker (Debian-based)
- **Database Backend**: FalkorDB
- **LLM Provider & Model**: Anthropic claude-haiku-4-5-20251001

## Installation Method
- [x] Docker (`zepai/knowledge-graph-mcp:1.0.2-graphiti-0.28.2`)

## Root Cause

`graphiti_mcp_server.py` lines 225-231 and 233-239 construct `Graphiti(...)` passing `llm_client` and `embedder` but not `cross_encoder`:

```python
self.client = Graphiti(
    graph_driver=falkor_driver,
    llm_client=llm_client,
    embedder=embedder_client,
    max_coroutines=self.semaphore_limit,
    # cross_encoder is missing here
)
```

`Graphiti.__init__` (graphiti.py line 142) accepts an optional `cross_encoder` parameter, but when it's not provided, it defaults to `OpenAIRerankerClient()` (line 224), which unconditionally requires `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

## Workaround

Monkey-patch `Graphiti.__init__` to inject an alternative reranker before the server starts. For example, for Gemini:

```python
import graphiti_core.graphiti as _graphiti

_orig_init = _graphiti.Graphiti.__init__

def _patched_init(self, *args, cross_encoder=None, **kwargs):
    if cross_encoder is None:
        from graphiti_core.cross_encoder.gemini_reranker_client import GeminiRerankerClient
        cross_encoder = GeminiRerankerClient()
    _orig_init(self, *args, cross_encoder=cross_encoder, **kwargs)

_graphiti.Graphiti.__init__ = _patched_init
```

## Possible Solution

graphiti-core already ships `GeminiRerankerClient` and `BGERerankerClient` alongside `OpenAIRerankerClient`. The MCP server could:

1. Add a `reranker` (or `cross_encoder`) section to the config schema, mirroring the existing `llm`/`embedder` pattern.
2. Or, as a simpler default, infer the reranker from the configured LLM provider (e.g., Anthropic/Gemini LLM → `GeminiRerankerClient`, OpenAI → `OpenAIRerankerClient`).
3. Pass the resulting `cross_encoder` to the `Graphiti()` constructor.

## Related

- #834 — `OpenAIRerankerClient` ignoring model config (closed, narrower scope)
- #517 — User confusion about configuring non-OpenAI providers in MCP Docker setup

title: [BUG] MCP Server Docker image missing optional provider extras (anthropic, google-genai, groq)
body:
## Bug Description

The MCP server Docker image (`zepai/knowledge-graph-mcp:1.0.2-graphiti-0.28.2`) installs `graphiti-core` without optional extras. This means non-OpenAI LLM providers (Anthropic, Gemini, Groq) fail at runtime even though they are listed as supported in the config schema and README.

The MCP server config accepts `provider: "anthropic"` (and gemini, groq), and the factory code in `services/factories.py` has code paths for these providers guarded by `HAS_ANTHROPIC`, `HAS_GEMINI`, `HAS_GROQ` flags. But since the extras aren't installed, these flags are `False` and the providers fail immediately.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Pull the latest MCP server image:
   ```
   docker pull zepai/knowledge-graph-mcp:1.0.2-graphiti-0.28.2
   ```

2. Configure `config.yaml` with an Anthropic provider:
   ```yaml
   llm:
     provider: "anthropic"
     model: "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001"
     temperature: 0.0
     providers:
       anthropic:
         api_key: "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}"
   ```

3. Start the server. It fails during initialization.

## Expected Behavior

The Docker image should include optional extras for all providers that the MCP server advertises as supported, so that switching providers is a config-only change.

## Actual Behavior

```
WARNING - Failed to create LLM client: Anthropic client not available in current graphiti-core version
```

The `HAS_ANTHROPIC` flag in `factories.py` is `False` because `graphiti-core[anthropic]` was not installed. Same applies to `HAS_GEMINI` and `HAS_GROQ`.

## Environment
- **Graphiti Version**: graphiti-core 0.28.2, MCP server 1.0.2 (Docker image `zepai/knowledge-graph-mcp:1.0.2-graphiti-0.28.2`)
- **Python Version**: 3.11
- **Operating System**: Docker (Debian-based)
- **Database Backend**: FalkorDB
- **LLM Provider & Model**: Anthropic claude-haiku-4-5-20251001

## Installation Method
- [x] Docker (`zepai/knowledge-graph-mcp:1.0.2-graphiti-0.28.2`)

## Workaround

Build a custom image that installs the extras. The image uses `uv`:

```dockerfile
FROM zepai/knowledge-graph-mcp:1.0.2-graphiti-0.28.2
RUN cd /app/mcp && uv add "graphiti-core[anthropic,google-genai]==0.28.2"
```

## Possible Solution

Change the Dockerfile for `zepai/knowledge-graph-mcp` to install graphiti-core with all optional provider extras:

```
graphiti-core[anthropic,google-genai,groq]==0.28.2
```

The additional dependencies are lightweight (the `anthropic`, `google-genai`, and `groq` Python packages) and would make the image work out of the box for all supported providers.

## Related

- #1393 — MCP server also doesn't configure the cross-encoder for non-OpenAI providers
- #517 — User confusion about configuring non-OpenAI providers in MCP Docker setup

title: add_episode tuple-unpack fails when extracted node count is not exactly 2
body:
# `add_episode` crashes with `ValueError: too many / not enough values to unpack` when extracted node count is not exactly 2

## Summary

In `graphiti_core/graphiti.py` line 992, the `update_communities`
branch of `add_episode()` does:

```python
communities, community_edges = await semaphore_gather(
    *[
        update_community(self.driver, self.llm_client, self.embedder, node)
        for node in nodes
    ],
    max_coroutines=self.max_coroutines,
)
```

`semaphore_gather` returns a list of N tuples (one per coroutine),
where each tuple is `(list[CommunityNode], list[CommunityEdge])`
(from `update_community`'s return type in
`graphiti_core/utils/maintenance/community_operations.py:326`). The
destructuring `communities, community_edges = <list of N tuples>`
treats the list as an iterable of length 2, so:

- **N == 2** → lucky coincidence: `communities` becomes the first
  tuple and `community_edges` becomes the second. The types are
  now wrong (both are tuples, not lists) but Python doesn't notice
  until a downstream consumer uses them.
- **N == 1** → `ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1)`
- **N == 3+** → `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)`

Any episode that happens to extract a number of entity nodes other
than exactly 2 will crash the whole `add_episode` call when
`update_communities=True` (the default).

## Environment

- graphiti-core 0.28.2 (PyPI)
- Python 3.12
- FalkorDB driver
- Any LLM backend

## Reproducer

```python
import asyncio
from graphiti_core import Graphiti
from graphiti_core.nodes import EpisodeType
from datetime import datetime, timezone

async def main():
    g = Graphiti(
        uri='falkor://localhost:6379',
        # ... your credentials ...
    )
    await g.build_indices_and_constraints()

    # Craft an episode that extracts exactly 1 entity — e.g. a
    # short sentence that only mentions one person:
    await g.add_episode(
        name='solo',
        episode_body='Alice went to the store.',
        source=EpisodeType.text,
        source_description='test',
        reference_time=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
        group_id='test',
        # update_communities defaults to True
    )

asyncio.run(main())
```

Expected: episode added cleanly.

Observed:
```
ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1)
  File ".../graphiti_core/graphiti.py", line 992, in add_episode
    communities, community_edges = await semaphore_gather(
```

Try again with an episode that extracts 3 entities
("Alice, Bob, and Carol went to the store together.") — same crash,
different message: `too many values to unpack (expected 2)`.

## Root cause

`update_community` in `community_operations.py:326` returns
`tuple[list[CommunityNode], list[CommunityEdge]]` — two parallel
lists **per node**. `semaphore_gather` returns a list of these tuples,
one per coroutine. The caller needs to flatten them, not unpack them
as if they were two top-level parallel lists.

## Suggested fix

```python
# graphiti.py:992
if update_communities:
    per_node_results = await semaphore_gather(
        *[
            update_community(self.driver, self.llm_client, self.embedder, node)
            for node in nodes
        ],
        max_coroutines=self.max_coroutines,
    )
    communities: list[CommunityNode] = []
    community_edges: list[CommunityEdge] = []
    for node_communities, node_community_edges in per_node_results:
        communities.extend(node_communities)
        community_edges.extend(node_community_edges)
```

This correctly accumulates the lists across all nodes regardless of
how many were extracted from the episode.

## Our workaround

We set `update_communities=False` on every `add_episode` call from
our application code (`lilly/graphiti_writer.py` and
`services/graphiti-mcp`). This means we don't benefit from
incremental community updates on ingest, but we work around the
crash. We rebuild communities in a nightly `build_communities()`
task instead (which has its own issues — see issue #3 and #4 in
this series).

## Impact

Any caller who uses the default `update_communities=True` and whose
episodes extract any number of entities other than exactly 2 will
hit this. It's surprising that the bug survives because lots of
two-participant conversational episodes happen to extract exactly
2 entities and work by accident.

## Labels suggestion

`bug`, `add_episode`, `community`
author: rmulligan

title: label_propagation has unbounded while True, oscillates forever on mid-sized graphs
body:
# `label_propagation` has unbounded `while True` and can oscillate forever on mid-sized graphs

## Summary

`graphiti_core/utils/maintenance/community_operations.py::label_propagation`
contains an unbounded `while True:` loop with no iteration cap. On
any graph where two or more adjacent nodes have tied neighbor counts,
the tiebreaker rule `new_community = max(community_candidate, curr_community)`
combined with the deterministic update order causes pairs of nodes
to flip each other's community labels on every pass without ever
converging.

We observed this on a **1,286-entity / 2,051-edge** graph: the
function ran for **44 minutes at 100% CPU with zero database
activity** before we killed the build. Python flame graph showed
100% of the time in `label_propagation`'s inner `community_candidates`
defaultdict accumulation loop — no I/O, no LLM calls, no GC, just
pure Python churn on tie flipping.

## Environment

- graphiti-core 0.28.2
- Python 3.12
- FalkorDB driver
- Graph: 1,286 entities, 2,051 edges built up over ~2 weeks of
  autonomous agent ingest

## Source (community_operations.py:92-137)

```python
def label_propagation(projection: dict[str, list[Neighbor]]) -> list[list[str]]:
    # Implement the label propagation community detection algorithm.
    # 1. Start with each node being assigned its own community
    # 2. Each node will take on the community of the plurality of its neighbors
    # 3. Ties are broken by going to the largest community
    # 4. Continue until no communities change during propagation

    community_map = {uuid: i for i, uuid in enumerate(projection.keys())}

    while True:                                          # <-- unbounded loop
        no_change = True
        new_community_map: dict[str, int] = {}

        for uuid, neighbors in projection.items():
            curr_community = community_map[uuid]

            community_candidates: dict[int, int] = defaultdict(int)
            for neighbor in neighbors:
                community_candidates[community_map[neighbor.node_uuid]] += neighbor.edge_count
            community_lst = [
                (count, community) for community, count in community_candidates.items()
            ]

            community_lst.sort(reverse=True)
            candidate_rank, community_candidate = community_lst[0] if community_lst else (0, -1)
            if community_candidate != -1 and candidate_rank > 1:
                new_community = community_candidate
            else:
                new_community = max(community_candidate, curr_community)   # <-- tiebreaker

            new_community_map[uuid] = new_community

            if new_community != curr_community:
                no_change = False

        if no_change:
            break

        community_map = new_community_map
    # ...
```

## Why it oscillates

Consider two nodes `A` and `B` connected by an edge with weight 1.
Initial assignment: `A=0, B=1`.

Iteration 1:
- Update `A`: its only neighbor is `B` with community 1. Rank 1, not
  > 1, so hits the tiebreaker: `new_community = max(1, 0) = 1`.
  `A → 1`.
- Update `B`: its only neighbor is `A`, which in `community_map`
  (not `new_community_map`!) still shows `0`. Rank 1, not > 1,
  tiebreaker: `new_community = max(0, 1) = 1`. `B → 1`.

Iteration 2 with `community_map = {A: 1, B: 1}`:
- Update `A`: neighbor `B` has community 1. Tiebreaker: `max(1, 1) = 1`.
  `A → 1`. No change.
- Update `B`: same. No change.
- `no_change = True`, break.

So for a trivially symmetric two-node case, it converges in 2
iterations. The problem is non-symmetric cases where the update
order causes asymmetric flips. On our observed graph, the result
was a persistent oscillation with `no_change` never reaching `True`.

A second reason the tiebreaker fails to converge: `max(community_candidate, curr_community)`
prefers higher-numbered communities, but the initial assignment
gives each node a community index equal to its position in the
projection dict. If the iteration order is stable (Python 3.7+),
this can create a systematic bias that flips nodes back and forth.

## Reproducer

The simplest repro we observed is running `build_communities()` on
a live knowledge graph with ~1,000+ loosely-connected nodes. A
synthetic repro requires a specific edge topology; we haven't
narrowed down the minimum-viable graph yet, but we can share an
export of the FalkorDB graph that triggers it (2.8 MB dump) if
that would help.

If you want an algorithmic test, Erdős–Rényi random graphs at
`n=1000, p=0.005` tend to produce the oscillation pattern.

## Suggested fix

Two complementary changes:

1. **Add an iteration cap.** Real-world label propagation on
   well-structured graphs converges in fewer than 20 iterations.
   A cap of 200 is a safety ceiling — if we hit it, the labels are
   approximate but the build moves forward instead of hanging.

   ```python
   MAX_ITERATIONS = 200

   for iteration in range(MAX_ITERATIONS):
       no_change = True
       new_community_map: dict[str, int] = {}
       # ... body ...
       if no_change:
           logger.info('label_propagation converged in %d iterations', iteration + 1)
           break
       community_map = new_community_map
   else:
       logger.warning(
           'label_propagation hit the %d-iteration safety cap without '
           'converging; community labels are approximate', MAX_ITERATIONS,
       )
       community_map = new_community_map
   ```

2. **Fix the tiebreaker** to prefer stability over bias.
   Instead of `max(community_candidate, curr_community)`, prefer
   `curr_community` when the rank is tied — this is how the
   reference label-propagation algorithm is usually specified,
   and it short-circuits oscillation almost entirely:

   ```python
   if community_candidate != -1 and candidate_rank > 1:
       new_community = community_candidate
   else:
       # Prefer the current community when tied — avoids oscillation
       new_community = curr_community if community_candidate in community_candidates else community_candidate
   ```

## Our workaround

We monkey-patch `label_propagation` with an iteration-capped version
before calling `graphiti.build_communities()`. Full patch available
at `scripts/build_communities.py::_apply_label_propagation_patch`.
Cap is 200, converges in <20 on healthy graphs, hits the cap and
logs a warning on pathological ones.

## Impact

For any graph that hits the oscillation pattern, `build_communities`
hangs indefinitely (we killed ours at 44 minutes). This is a
production-blocking issue for anyone using Graphiti's community
feature at scale, and we suspect many users never notice because
they silently run out of patience and kill the build.

## Labels suggestion

`bug`, `performance`, `community`, `infinite loop`
author: rmulligan

title: build_communities ignores Graphiti.max_coroutines; nested semaphore_gather falls back to env var
body:
# `build_communities` ignores `Graphiti.max_coroutines`; nested `semaphore_gather` falls back to env var

## Summary

`graphiti_core/utils/maintenance/community_operations.py::build_communities`
has two nested parallelism layers:

1. **Outer**: `build_communities` itself wraps each cluster in a
   `limited_build_community` coroutine and gathers them using a
   hardcoded `asyncio.Semaphore(MAX_COMMUNITY_BUILD_CONCURRENCY)`.
   The constant is `10` and is not configurable at runtime.

2. **Inner**: within each `build_community`, the pairwise
   `summarize_pair` LLM calls are themselves fan-out via
   `semaphore_gather(...)` **with no `max_coroutines` argument**.
   That falls through to `SEMAPHORE_LIMIT = int(os.getenv('SEMAPHORE_LIMIT', 20))`
   in `graphiti_core/helpers.py:38`, which is read at module import
   time.

Neither layer consults `Graphiti.max_coroutines`. So a caller who
sets `graphiti.max_coroutines = 2` to throttle LLM requests under
a rate-limited backend has **no effect** on community build
concurrency — the outer layer fires 10 clusters in parallel and
each of those fires up to 20 LLM calls in parallel, for a peak
burst of 200 concurrent LLM requests.

## Environment

- graphiti-core 0.28.2
- Python 3.12
- Local LLM backend (llama.cpp via llama-swap) with 2-slot
  parallelism, 3-slot breaker at the application layer

## Source

### Outer layer (community_operations.py:217-244)

```python
MAX_COMMUNITY_BUILD_CONCURRENCY = 10   # hardcoded module-level constant

async def build_communities(
    driver: GraphDriver,
    llm_client: LLMClient,
    group_ids: list[str] | None,
) -> tuple[list[CommunityNode], list[CommunityEdge]]:
    community_clusters = await get_community_clusters(driver, group_ids)

    semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(MAX_COMMUNITY_BUILD_CONCURRENCY)

    async def limited_build_community(cluster):
        async with semaphore:
            return await build_community(llm_client, cluster)

    communities = list(
        await semaphore_gather(
            *[limited_build_community(c) for c in community_clusters]
            # <-- no max_coroutines passed; semaphore_gather falls
            #     back to SEMAPHORE_LIMIT env var (default 20)
        )
    )
```

### Inner layer (community_operations.py:184)

```python
async def build_community(llm_client, community_cluster):
    summaries = [entity.summary for entity in community_cluster]
    length = len(summaries)
    while length > 1:
        # ...
        new_summaries = list(
            await semaphore_gather(
                *[
                    summarize_pair(llm_client, (str(left_summary), str(right_summary)))
                    for left_summary, right_summary in zip(
                        summaries[: int(length / 2)], summaries[int(length / 2) :], strict=False
                    )
                ]
                # <-- same omission; no max_coroutines, falls back to env
            )
        )
```

### Fallback (helpers.py:123-133)

```python
SEMAPHORE_LIMIT = int(os.getenv('SEMAPHORE_LIMIT', 20))

async def semaphore_gather(
    *coroutines: Coroutine,
    max_coroutines: int | None = None,
) -> list[Any]:
    semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(max_coroutines or SEMAPHORE_LIMIT)
    # ...
```

`SEMAPHORE_LIMIT` is captured at module import time, so changing
the env var after importing has no effect.

## Reproducer

```python
import os
# Attempt 1: set max_coroutines on the client — expected to throttle build
import asyncio
from graphiti_core import Graphiti

async def main():
    g = Graphiti(uri='...', ...)
    g.max_coroutines = 2   # Expect: build_communities respects this
    # Actual: build fans out 10×20 = 200 concurrent LLM calls at peak
    nodes, edges = await g.build_communities(group_ids=['test'])

asyncio.run(main())
```

On a rate-limited backend this trips the breaker (we saw
`RateLimitError` from our llama-swap at ~30 concurrent requests
when `g.max_coroutines=2` was supposedly in force).

To actually throttle, you must set the env var **before importing
graphiti_core**:

```python
import os
os.environ['SEMAPHORE_LIMIT'] = '1'  # MUST be set before graphiti_core imports
import graphiti_core
```

## Impact

Any caller whose LLM backend has a concurrency cap — most local
llama.cpp setups, cloud backends with rate limits, paid APIs with
TPM caps — gets burnt by `build_communities` bursting past their
limit. The user-visible symptom is `RateLimitError` from the
backend, or silent failures from circuit breakers, and the
apparent fix (`graphiti.max_coroutines = N`) doesn't work because
neither of the nested gathers honor it.

## Suggested fix

Thread `max_coroutines` through the nested gathers:

```python
# build_communities
async def build_communities(
    driver: GraphDriver,
    llm_client: LLMClient,
    group_ids: list[str] | None,
    max_coroutines: int | None = None,          # new param
) -> tuple[list[CommunityNode], list[CommunityEdge]]:
    community_clusters = await get_community_clusters(driver, group_ids)

    # Outer throttle: use caller's limit or fall back to module default
    outer_limit = max_coroutines or MAX_COMMUNITY_BUILD_CONCURRENCY
    semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(outer_limit)

    async def limited_build_community(cluster):
        async with semaphore:
            return await build_community(llm_client, cluster, max_coroutines=max_coroutines)

    communities = list(
        await semaphore_gather(
            *[limited_build_community(c) for c in community_clusters],
            max_coroutines=outer_limit,
        )
    )
    # ...


# build_community
async def build_community(
    llm_client: LLMClient,
    community_cluster: list[EntityNode],
    max_coroutines: int | None = None,           # new param
) -> tuple[CommunityNode, list[CommunityEdge]]:
    # ...
    new_summaries = list(
        await semaphore_gather(
            *[
                summarize_pair(llm_client, (str(l), str(r)))
                for l, r in zip(...)
            ],
            max_coroutines=max_coroutines,         # thread through
        )
    )
```

And then at the call site in `Graphiti`, `graphiti.py` or wherever
`build_communities` is invoked, pass `max_coroutines=self.max_coroutines`.

This preserves backward compatibility (default falls back to
existing constants) while giving callers a way to actually
throttle parallelism.

## Our workaround

Set `SEMAPHORE_LIMIT=1` environment variable **before** importing
`graphiti_core`:

```python
import os
os.environ['SEMAPHORE_LIMIT'] = '1'  # CRITICAL: must be before graphiti_core import

# ... rest of imports ...
from graphiti_core import Graphiti
```

This serializes all `semaphore_gather` calls in the process, not
just community build. For our use case (nightly `build_communities`
as a dedicated process), that's acceptable. For a long-running
service process, serializing all graphiti concurrency is too
aggressive.

## Labels suggestion

`bug`, `performance`, `rate limiting`, `community`
author: rmulligan

title: build_communities crashes on nested attribute values with Neo4j (TypeError: Property values can only be of primitive types)
body:
### Summary

When the LLM extraction path produces entities or edges with nested `Map`/`List` attributes (e.g. a dict of lists, or a list of dicts), writing them to Neo4j via the bulk path raises:

```
Neo.ClientError.Statement.TypeError
Property values can only be of primitive types or arrays thereof.
Encountered: Map{...}
```

and the whole `build_communities` / bulk-add call fails. The Kuzu backend already handles this case by serializing attributes — Neo4j needs the same treatment.

### Reproduction

Any extraction that yields a nested attribute. Minimal example: an entity whose extracted attributes look like `{"metadata": {"tags": ["x", "y"]}}` or `{"history": [{"year": 2020, "event": "..."}]}`.

### Expected

Nested attributes round-trip through Neo4j without crashing the write, matching the Kuzu backend's behavior.

### Actual

Neo4j rejects the write because attributes are currently spread as individual node properties instead of serialized.

### Proposed fix

I've opened #1109 with a fix that serializes attributes to JSON for the Neo4j write path (mirroring what `bulk_utils.py` already does for Kuzu) and updates the read path to transparently handle both JSON strings and the legacy dict format, so existing data keeps working. The PR has been waiting for review since December — happy to rebase or adjust the approach if there's a different direction you'd prefer.
author: Ataxia123

title: build_communities hangs forever on hub-and-spoke graphs (label_propagation infinite oscillation)
body:
### Summary

`label_propagation` in `graphiti_core/utils/maintenance/community_operations.py` uses **synchronous batch updates**: it snapshots the community map at the start of each pass, computes new labels for every node from that snapshot, then replaces the map wholesale. On graphs with high-degree hub nodes, tied candidate scores cause groups of nodes to swap labels symmetrically every iteration, producing a flip-flop that never converges. The `while True:` loop at the top of the function never terminates.

### Reproduction

A 48-entity knowledge graph with a central hub connected to 14+ peers reliably hangs. 19 of the 48 nodes keep flipping between two community assignments indefinitely. The hang happens inside a synchronous function with no yield points, so it freezes the caller completely — in our deployment it hung a FastAPI worker serving `build_communities`, and no `try`/`except` in the call chain could recover it.

### Expected

`label_propagation` converges on all graphs, including hub-heavy ones. This is a well-known property of the **asynchronous** form of LPA described in Raghavan, Albert, Kumara (2007), _Near linear time algorithm to detect community structures in large-scale networks_.

### Actual

Synchronous batch LPA is vulnerable to the oscillation pattern on hub graphs. The bug reproduces 100% of the time on the minimized test case and also reproduced in production.

### Proposed fix

I've opened #1388 with the asynchronous LPA form plus a small cycle detector as a belt-and-suspenders safeguard. It includes a test suite covering the regression case, several common graph shapes, and a deterministic-seed test. The original 48-node hang now converges in milliseconds. Happy to adjust the approach if there's a different direction you'd prefer.
author: Ataxia123

title: build_communities LLM cost scales O(total_nodes), blocking use on large graphs
body:
### Summary

`build_community` feeds every member's summary into a binary-tree pairwise merge, calling `summarize_pair` once per pair. For a community of N members that's N−1 LLM calls plus a final `generate_summary_description`. Across the whole graph, the total summary cost scales as **O(total_nodes)** regardless of how the graph partitions.

On a 100k-node knowledge graph that's roughly **100k LLM calls** per `build_communities` run, which makes the operation cost-prohibitive at scale even though the underlying clustering finishes in seconds. The pricing barrier effectively caps the size of graphs where communities can be kept fresh.

### Proposal

Add an optional `sample_size: int | None = None` parameter to `build_communities` (and the internal `build_community`). When set, each community ranks its members and feeds only the top-K into the binary merge. Reasonable ranking:

1. In-community weighted degree descending — hub nodes carry the community's structural signal
2. Summary length descending — entities with rich summaries contribute more useful content
3. Name as deterministic tie-breaker

The in-community degree can be computed from the projection `get_community_clusters` already builds during clustering, so there are no extra queries. Default behavior (no sampling) is unchanged, so existing deployments are unaffected.

Total cost becomes **O(num_communities × sample_size)** instead of O(total_nodes) — e.g. communities averaging 200 members with `sample_size=10` is a 20× reduction.

### Empirical results

On a 48-entity test graph with `sample_size=5`:

| Metric | Full | Sampled (k=5) |
|---|---|---|
| Wall time | 41.2s | 13.3s (3.1× faster) |
| Communities found | 13 | 13 (identical) |
| Member edges | 48 | 48 (identical) |
| LLM calls | ~50 | ~15 |

Sampled summary quality was equal-or-better in every community, notably sharper on the largest one (where diluting across 26 members had been producing a bland list of exits; the top-5 sample named the location and described its atmosphere).

### Proposed implementation

I've opened #1389 with the `sample_size` parameter, the ranking helper, an 8-test unit suite, and an end-to-end check against a real Neo4j-backed graph. Happy to adjust scope or rename things if there's a preferred shape.

title: Meeting intelligence extraction pipeline into Graphiti storage
body:
Graphiti's temporal knowledge graph is impressive — the time-aware entity tracking is exactly what's missing from most knowledge systems.

I would like to propose a complementary pipeline using [Kernal](https://github.com/pintomatic/kernal) as the extraction layer feeding into Graphiti as the storage layer.

**Kernal** specializes in extracting structured entities (people, organizations, relationships, deals, goals) from natural conversation — particularly meeting transcripts. It handles the messy NLP to structured data step.

**Graphiti** excels at storing those entities with temporal validity and enabling traversal queries.

The pipeline: Raw transcript → Kernal extracts entities with timestamps → feeds structured data into Graphiti with time validity → enables queries like "What was our relationship with Acme Corp in Q3 vs Q4?"

Both projects are open-source and could benefit from a shared extraction to storage pattern. Interested in exploring this?
